title: VCF Automation 9.1 Go client: reference-derived contract, token refresh mid-run, contract-pinned mock
prompt:
We need a small Go client for the VCF Automation API in VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 — the product that replaced vRealize and Aria Automation.

The repository is scaffolded. `contract/` is finished: it defines and validates the contract format. `automation/`, `mock/` and `wire/` declare their exported API and return `errNotImplemented`. `docs/` is empty. Read `README.md` and `docs/README.md` before you start; the exported signatures are fixed, everything unexported is yours.

There are four things to deliver.

## 1. `docs/contract.json` and `docs/official_sources.json`

VCF Automation has no machine-readable specification. It is absent from the `vmware/vcf-api-specs` repository and there is no OpenAPI document to generate from or validate against. What exists is the xAPIs reference documentation on developer.broadcom.com, a page per operation.

Work out from those pages the five operations listed in `docs/README.md`: the exact method and path template of each, its path and query parameters, its request body fields where it has one, and its success response shape. Mark as optional what the reference marks optional, and record the defaults it documents — the mock applies them and the client relies on them.

Then record where each of it came from. `docs/official_sources.json` takes one record per operation per page consulted: the operation, the page URL, that page's own title, and the date you read it. And say plainly in the contract's `source` block that this was transcribed from reference documentation rather than from a published specification — that is the only durable signal to a later reader that these names carry no machine-checked guarantee behind them.

Take the values from the reference pages themselves. Do not carry the Aria Automation 8.x shapes over from memory: several of them changed in 9.x, and some of what the portal still lists is deprecated in favour of something else.

## 2. The client, `automation/`

Implement the declared API, building requests from the loaded contract rather than from string literals, so that the client and the mock cannot drift apart independently.

The scenario that matters is token expiry. The service issues short-lived access tokens, and a long run outlives its token. The client holds a long-lived API token, exchanges it for an access token, and must notice when the service stops accepting that access token, exchange again, and carry on — without the caller ever seeing the interruption, without discarding results already collected, and without redoing work already done. The client is used concurrently: goroutines that meet the same expired token at the same moment must cause one exchange between them, not one each.

## 3. The mock, `mock/`

A loopback stand-in for an appliance, pinned to the contract. It serves only the operations the contract names, rejects query parameters and body fields the contract does not declare, and logs every request it receives — including the ones it rejects — so that a test can read back exactly what went on the wire. The order it applies routing, validation and authentication in is documented in `mock/server.go`; the acceptance suite depends on it.

## 4. The verifier, `wire/`

Given a logged request and an expectation, report every way in which they differ, not just the first.

Exactness matters in both directions: a query parameter or body key the expectation does not list must not have been sent at all. Nearly every body field in this API is optional, so the bug worth catching is a client that sends `""`, `0` or `null` for a field the caller never set. That is a different request from omitting the field, and the verifier has to say which of the two it found, in as many words. A value the caller deliberately set to the zero value of its type must still be sent.

## Testing

Cover `automation`, `mock` and `wire` with table-driven tests. Everything must pass under `go test -race ./...`. Nothing in the suite may contact a VMware endpoint — the loopback mock is the only server the tests talk to.

`verification/` is the acceptance suite; treat it as read-only. Run `bash verification/run.sh` to check your work.
